![Trinity (bold, rightmost in each panel) tops every single-model and multi-agent baseline across MATH500, MMLU, RLPR, and LiveCodeBench, approaching the per-question-best oracle. Figure 3 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="cover-full.jpg"}

In *TRINITY: An Evolved LLM Coordinator* [[1]](#ref-1) (ICLR 2026), [Jinglue Xu](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2397339171), [Qi Sun](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2326487319), [Peter Schwendeman](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2396352279), [Stefan Nielsen](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2396336821), [Edoardo Cetin](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2326294214), and [Yujin Tang](https://www.semanticscholar.org/author/2326422916) (Sakana AI, University of Michigan, and Institute of Science Tokyo) train a 0.6B *coordinator* that learns to delegate each turn of a query to one of seven larger LLMs and assign it a role, instead of answering the query itself.

> Combining diverse foundation models is promising, but weight-merging is limited by mismatched architectures and closed APIs. Trinity addresses this with *a lightweight coordinator that orchestrates collaboration among large language models (LLMs)*. The coordinator, comprising a compact language model (approximately $0.6$B parameters) and a lightweight head (approximately $10$K parameters), is optimized with an *evolutionary strategy* for efficient and adaptive delegation. Trinity processes queries over multiple turns, where at each turn the coordinator *assigns one of three roles (Thinker, Worker, or Verifier) to a selected LLM*, effectively offloading complex skill acquisition from the coordinator itself. Experiments show that Trinity consistently outperforms individual models and existing methods across coding, math, reasoning, and domain knowledge tasks, and generalizes robustly to out-of-distribution tasks. On standard benchmarks, Trinity achieves state-of-the-art results, including *a score of 86.2% on LiveCodeBench*. Theoretical and empirical analyses identify two main factors behind this performance: (1) the coordinator's hidden-state representations provide rich contextualization of inputs, and (2) under high dimensionality and strict budget constraints, *the separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy* offers advantages over reinforcement learning, imitation learning, and random search by exploiting potential *block-$\epsilon$-separability*.

## Methods

The contribution is a small, cheap-to-train coordinator placed in front of a pool of larger models, deciding who does what each turn. The harder problem is how to train it, because the right decision has no labels. The paper rules out supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in turn, then trains the coordinator with a black-box evolution strategy.

### The coordinator

- **A 0.6B coordinator with a ~10K-parameter head.** Two pieces are trained on top of a frozen Qwen3-0.6B small language model (SLM):
  - **The selection head.** A lightweight head (~10K parameters) runs beside the SLM's usual language-model head. At each turn it reads the hidden state at the penultimate output-token position and emits two sets of logits: one selects an LLM from the pool, the other assigns it a *role*.
  - **Singular value fine-tuning (SVF).** The other trained piece rescales the singular values of the SLM's weight matrices, leaving the rest of the base model frozen. SVF is carried over from the same group's earlier [*Transformer-Squared*](/posts/20260629-transformer-squared/) [[2]](#ref-2), which adapts a model by rescaling existing singular values rather than adding new parameters. Transformer² trained those scales with reinforcement learning. Trinity keeps the parametrization but swaps in an evolution strategy, for the reasons in the next section.
- **Three roles, assigned per turn.** A query runs over up to five turns. On each turn the chosen LLM is cast as a *Thinker* (decompose the problem), a *Worker* (perform a step), or a *Verifier* (check the running answer and flag edge cases), and a message-processing module injects the matching role prompt before the call. Figure 1 walks through a depreciation problem: a Thinker decomposes it on turn 1, a Worker computes on turn 2, a Verifier checks the result on turn 3.

![The coordination architecture (left) and a worked three-turn example (right): a compact SLM plus a lightweight head select an LLM and a role each turn, then route the role-specific prompt to the chosen model. Figure 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure1.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure1-full.png"}

![The coordinator's parametrization: the lightweight head runs beside the base model's LM head and reads the penultimate output-token hidden state, emitting one set of logits to select an LLM and another to assign a role. The singular-value scales of the SLM's weight matrices (red diagonals) are also fine-tuned. Figure 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure2.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure2-full.png"}

- **A linear head is enough, because the representation is already separable.** A linear SVM sorts the SLM's penultimate-token hidden states into the four task types at 100%, far above the 25% chance line (Figure 5). With the representation that well-structured, a small linear head has enough signal to read off coordination decisions.

![Task-type separability of the SLM's penultimate-token hidden states. Left: a linear SVM separates the four task types at 100%, far above the 25% chance line. Right: t-SNE shows the same four types as clean clusters. Figure 5 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure5.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure5-full.png"}

### Why an evolution strategy, not RL or SFT

This is the paper's central design choice. The coordinator's target, which LLM to call and which role to assign each turn, has no ground truth. The only signal is a binary pass/fail reward earned by running the full multi-turn pipeline end to end, so there is nothing to fit with supervised learning directly. The paper works through the alternatives:

- **Synthetic labels plus SFT: ruled out by cost.** One option is to manufacture labels, running the whole pool on each question and taking the per-question-best model, then fine-tuning on them. That is feasible for a single step but explodes in the multi-turn setting (up to five turns, seven models, three roles), where the paper estimates label generation at roughly $10^{11}$ LLM calls.
- **Reinforcement learning: ruled out by low-signal gradients.** REINFORCE is the natural label-free optimizer, but the ~10K parameters are weakly coupled, so each one barely moves the scalar reward. Under a binary reward and a tight budget its per-parameter gradients are too low-signal to learn from, and random search does worse, collapsing onto a single agent and role.
- **The choice: separable CMA-ES.** SVF fixes *which* parameters move, the singular-value scales plus the head. The optimizer is *how* they move: Trinity searches that parameter vector with the separable [Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy](/posts/20260629-cma-es-primer/) (sep-CMA-ES), keeping a Gaussian over the parameters, sampling candidate vectors, scoring each by running the coordinator, and shifting the Gaussian toward the ones that scored better. It needs no labels and no gradient, and because it ranks whole parameter vectors instead of estimating a per-parameter gradient, it sidesteps the exact low-signal problem that makes REINFORCE ineffective here.
  - **Block-$\epsilon$-separability lets the cheap diagonal variant suffice.** The paper argues the objective splits into near-independent blocks, one per agent and role choice, that interact only weakly. The $\epsilon$ in the name bounds how much residual coupling remains across blocks. When that coupling is small, a diagonal covariance gives up almost nothing against a full one, so the cheap $O(n)$ sep-CMA-ES matches a full-covariance search that would cost $O(n^2)$.

The ablation in the Results section makes the choice concrete: at matched budget, sep-CMA-ES clears the REINFORCE, random-search, and SFT baselines on every in-distribution task.

## Results

Trinity coordinates a pool of seven LLMs: three closed (GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 4 Sonnet) and four open (Gemma 3 27B-IT, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and Qwen3-32B in direct and reasoning modes). It is trained and evaluated on four in-distribution tasks (MATH500 [[3]](#ref-3), MMLU [[4]](#ref-4), RLPR [[5]](#ref-5), and LiveCodeBench [[6]](#ref-6)) and tested zero-shot on four held-out tasks (AIME 2025 [[7]](#ref-7), BigCodeBench [[8]](#ref-8), MT-Bench [[9]](#ref-9), and GPQA-Diamond [[10]](#ref-10)). The baselines:

- each single model at its base budget and at a 5× context budget
- single-model five-turn self-reflection
- multi-agent methods: Mixture-of-Agents, RouterDC, and Smoothie

A per-question-best oracle (the union of correct answers across all seven models) marks the ceiling no coordinator over this pool can pass.

- **Beats every single model and multi-agent baseline in-distribution.** On the four training tasks Trinity tops all baselines (Figure 3, the cover) and comes close to the per-question-best oracle on MATH500 (0.88 against 0.91), MMLU (0.92 against 0.97), and LiveCodeBench (0.61 against 0.65). The gap to the oracle is widest on RLPR (0.41 against 0.61) [[1]](#ref-1).
- **Generalizes zero-shot to held-out tasks.** Averaged over the four held-out tasks (Table 1), Trinity scores 54.21, ahead of the strongest single models Gemini 2.5 Pro (52.34) and GPT-5 (51.07). It takes the top spot on AIME (50.00), MT-Bench (9.60), and GPQA-Diamond (76.82), and ties for first on BigCodeBench (35.80) [[1]](#ref-1).

![Results on the four held-out tasks, best per column in bold. Trinity (bottom row) posts the best average at 54.21, tops AIME, MT-Bench, and GPQA-Diamond, and ties Claude 4 Sonnet on BigCodeBench. Table 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table1.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="table1-full.png"}

- **Sets a LiveCodeBench record unconstrained.** In the unconstrained setting (Figure 4), Trinity reaches a pass@1 of 86.2% on LiveCodeBench V6 (newly released questions spanning January to April 2025), a new state of the art, and the score rises with the per-query turn budget.

![LiveCodeBench at full power: Trinity reaches a state-of-the-art pass@1 of 86.2% (top), and the score increases as the per-query turn budget grows (bottom). Figure 4 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure4.png){fig-align="center"}

- **Every component contributes to the score.** An ablation on the in-distribution tasks removes one piece at a time (Table 2): dropping the singular-value fine-tuning, the Thinker role, the tri-role selection, or the penultimate-token readout each lowers Trinity's average, and Trinity outscores all three closed single models head-to-head [[1]](#ref-1).

![Trinity (top) against four ablations and the three closed single models on the in-distribution tasks. Removing the singular-value fine-tuning, the Thinker role, the tri-role selection, or the penultimate-token readout each lowers the average, and Trinity beats all three single models. Table 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table2.png){fig-align="center"}

## My Notes

- **The evolution strategy beats their RL baseline at matched budget.** Trinity's optimizer comparison runs the same coordinator under four training methods at matched budget: REINFORCE scores 0.25 on LiveCodeBench and 0.46 on MATH500, while sep-CMA-ES reaches 0.62 and 0.88 [[1]](#ref-1). That ordering matches a long-standing finding that evolution strategies stay competitive with policy-gradient reinforcement learning when the reward is sparse or binary [[11]](#ref-11). It fits the regime here: a high-dimensional search over ~10K weakly coupled parameters, where REINFORCE's per-parameter gradients are too low-signal to learn from, against a pass/fail task reward. Sakana ships this evolution-trained coordinator as [Sakana Fugu](/posts/20260629-fugu-release/) [[12]](#ref-12), the everyday model in the product's two-model line: Fugu builds on Trinity, while the heavier Fugu-Ultra builds on the RL-trained [Conductor](/posts/20260629-conductor-llm-orchestrator/) [[15]](#ref-15). The two are separate models behind one endpoint rather than two stages of one orchestrator.
- **The 0.6B coordinator adds almost no capability of its own.** It trains only the ~10K head and freezes the base model, so the answer quality comes from the frontier models it calls. Trinity therefore cannot beat the per-question-best oracle, the best any single model in the pool already gets right. It applies the routing idea behind a [cost-routing triager](/posts/20260429-frontier-model-lower-bill/) to quality, and has the same limitation: it helps only when a capable model is already in the pool.
- **The coordinator builds the agentic graph dynamically, turn by turn.** Choosing an LLM and a role at each turn is the same as constructing the multi-agent topology on the fly: every step adds the next node for that specific query, rather than running a structure fixed in advance. Trinity is one of several recent systems that learn this structure rather than hand-build it: [MASS](/posts/20260430-multi-agent-system-search/) searches prompts and topologies offline into a fixed design [[13]](#ref-13), [MAPO](/posts/20260520-adaptive-collaboration-mapo/) trains a policy for when to defer [[14]](#ref-14), and Sakana's own pair builds it online, by reinforcement learning in [Conductor](/posts/20260629-conductor-llm-orchestrator/) [[15]](#ref-15) and by an evolution strategy here, then ships both behind one endpoint in [Sakana Fugu](/posts/20260629-fugu-release/) [[12]](#ref-12).

## Related Posts

- [Learning to Orchestrate Agents in Natural Language with the Conductor](/posts/20260629-conductor-llm-orchestrator/): the same group's sibling, which learns coordination by reinforcement learning at 7B rather than the evolution strategy Trinity runs on a 0.6B head.
- [Sakana Fugu: One Model to Command Them All](/posts/20260629-fugu-release/): the product whose two models extend this pair separately — the everyday Fugu builds on Trinity, the quality-first Fugu-Ultra builds on Conductor — behind one endpoint.
- [A Primer on the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES)](/posts/20260629-cma-es-primer/): the standing primer on the optimizer Trinity is trained with, covering what sep-CMA-ES is, why it beats gradient methods in this low-budget regime, and the diagonal variant Trinity uses.
- [Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies](/posts/20260430-multi-agent-system-search/): searches the prompts and topologies of a multi-agent system offline, the design Trinity instead learns online.
- [Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs](/posts/20260520-adaptive-collaboration-mapo/): trains a policy for when to defer, the delegation decision Trinity's coordinator makes every turn.
- [MAST: A Failure Taxonomy for Multi-Agent Systems](/posts/20250802-mast-multi-agent-failures/): catalogs how multi-agent pipelines break, the failure modes a learned coordinator has to route around.
